The initiative offers long-term, low-cost supplemental loans to help communities invest in drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater infrastructure, with the goal of protecting public health and the environment. The EPA is currently accepting letters of interest for both WIFIA and SWIFIA loans and is providing technical assistance to aid prospective borrowers, particularly small and disadvantaged communities, in developing their funding requests. Key priority areas for this funding round include investing in economically stressed communities, replacing lead service lines, addressing PFAS and other emerging contaminants, and mitigating the impacts of drought. <2> The Water Council's 2023 Water Leaders Summit was held in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, from September 13-14, 2023. [2, 3] The summit's theme was 'Building Water Resiliency,' and it convened water and sustainability professionals to discuss pressing water challenges, innovation, technology, and stewardship. [2, 3] A blog post discussing the event was published on September 19, 2023. [3] For 2024, The Water Council partnered with Marquette University's Sustainability Lab to create a new, combined event called the Nexus Sustainability Leaders Summit, [6, 13, 14] This new summit builds upon the legacy of the Water Leaders Summit and explores a broader range of topics including water, energy, finance, and ESG reporting. [13, 14] The second annual Nexus Sustainability Leaders Summit is scheduled for October 14-15, 2025. [5, 16] <3> A U.S. Drought Monitor report for the week of September 12, 2023, revealed that 31.1% of the United States and Puerto Rico was experiencing moderate to exceptional drought. This marked an increase from the 30.2% reported in the previous week. The most severe categories, encompassing extreme to exceptional drought, also expanded, rising from 7.5% to cover 8.0% of the nation. The report, a collaborative effort by the National Drought Mitigation Center, the USDA, and NOAA, identified predominantly drier than normal conditions across most of the West, the southern Plains, and the Mississippi and Ohio Valleys. <4> A U.S. Drought Monitor report from late August 2023 indicated that drought was impacting 40% of the Midwest region. Wisconsin was particularly affected, with a report on August 25, 2023, noting that 78% of the state was experiencing drought. For the first time since the U.S. Drought Monitor's inception in 2000, a portion of northern Wisconsin, specifically in Douglas and Bayfield counties, was placed in the highest category of exceptional drought (D4). This was attributed to a significant heatwave and lack of rainfall, which exacerbated conditions. The consequences included diminished soil moisture, poor pasture conditions that necessitated supplemental feed for livestock, and low water levels in streams, ponds, and major rivers like the Upper Mississippi. <5> In late August 2023, Texas grappled with a significant drought, as detailed in a report from the Texas Water Resources Institute. [4] According to the U.S. Drought Monitor's data from August 22, 2023, over 62% of the state was experiencing severe drought or worse, with nearly 34% in extreme drought conditions. [4] These arid conditions, intensified by the hottest August in Texas since 1895, led to considerable strain on water resources and agriculture. [4, 6] The impacts were widespread, causing stress on livestock, the drying of ponds, and reduced crop yields. [4] Consequently, many municipalities were compelled to implement water restrictions. [4] By the end of the month, 76% of the state was in some level of drought, a 27 percentage point increase from the end of July. [6] The state's water supply reservoirs were at approximately 69% capacity, over 13 percentage points below the normal level for that time of year. [6, 8] <6> In response to low streamflows in the Elwha River, the City of Port Angeles, Washington, declared a Stage II water shortage on August 22, 2023, asking residents to begin voluntary water conservation. The Clallam County Public Utility District (PUD) coordinated its response, also declaring a Stage 2 alert for the Gales Addition, Mount Angeles, and Monroe water systems which also draw from the Elwha River. The initial voluntary phase was part of a broader issue, with a report from late August 2023 indicating that 75% of all waterways in Washington were experiencing low streamflow conditions, and forecasts predicted a warmer, drier fall. Due to continuously decreasing river flows, the city escalated its response, declaring a mandatory Stage III water shortage on September 11, 2023, which prohibited certain non-essential outdoor water uses. <7> On August 15, 2023, the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation announced that the Colorado River will operate under a Tier 1 shortage for calendar year 2024. This determination was based on the projected water levels of Lake Mead and Lake Powell as detailed in the August 2023 24-Month Study. The Tier 1 declaration was an improvement from the more severe Tier 2 shortage condition that had been in place for 2023, a change largely attributed to above-average precipitation and conservation efforts. Under this shortage, Arizona and Nevada will have their water allocations reduced, and Mexico's delivery will also be cut in accordance with existing agreements. While the improved hydrology provided short-term relief, federal officials emphasized that the river system's combined reservoir storage was only at 36%, and long-term sustainability challenges persist due to a multi-decade drought and overuse. <8> A report from the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) confirmed that the national moderate-to-exceptional drought footprint across the contiguous U.S. increased during July 2023. According to the U.S. Drought Monitor, the area experiencing moderate to exceptional drought rose from 27.0% at the end of June to 28.08% by August 1, 2023. This was exacerbated by record-breaking heatwaves, particularly in the Southwest, which increased evapotranspiration. Arizona, New Mexico, Maine, and Florida all recorded their warmest July on record. For instance, Phoenix, Arizona, experienced 31 consecutive days with temperatures exceeding 110°F, contributing to the hottest month ever recorded for any U.S. city. The month was the 11th warmest July on record for the contiguous U.S. as a whole.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On January 30, 2024, New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham unveiled a 50-Year Water Action Plan to address the state's long-term water security. [2] This comprehensive strategy was developed in response to scientific projections indicating New Mexico's water supply will decrease by 25% over the next five decades. [2, 6] The plan, created with input from scientists, stakeholders, and various communities, focuses on three main pillars: expanding water conservation, developing new water sources, and improving water quality protections. [2] Key initiatives include a public education campaign to reduce urban water use, incentivizing modern irrigation technology to cut agricultural water consumption, creating a Strategic Water Supply to provide billions of gallons of new water for industries like clean energy, and implementing a new surface water discharge permitting program to protect rivers and lakes. [2, 5] <2> According to a U.S. Drought Monitor report published on January 25, 2024, as of January 23, 2024, moderate to exceptional drought covered 23.0% of the United States and Puerto Rico. This represented a decrease from the previous week's figure of 24.1%. Despite the reduction, abnormal dryness and drought were still affecting over 89 million people, accounting for approximately 28.6% of the population. <3> Based on reports from the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), drought conditions in the mainland Southeast intensified in November 2023 due to below-normal precipitation. [9] By late November, drought had expanded, with some areas in North Carolina experiencing Severe (D2) and Extreme (D3) drought for the first time since March 2017. [10] The Southern region, particularly Louisiana, Mississippi, southeastern Arkansas, and Tennessee, faced extremely dry conditions during the fall of 2023. [7] However, conditions began to improve in December 2023. A series of weather systems brought above-normal precipitation to parts of the interior Southeast, leading to a reduction in the intensity and coverage of the drought by the end of the year. [3, 4, 5] For instance, by the week of December 26, drought had contracted in parts of the Southeast due to recent rainfall. [4] Still, the Southern and Midwestern drought and associated heatwave were collectively the costliest weather event of 2023, amounting to $14.5 billion in damages. The announcement, made in Las Vegas, detailed specific agreements with the Coachella Valley Water District to save up to 105,000 acre-feet and with the Quechan Indian Tribe to save up to 39,000 acre-feet through 2025. These California agreements are in addition to 18 existing agreements with partners in Arizona aimed at conserving water in Lake Mead. [5, 7] Severely affected areas include the western United States, parts of India, northeastern China, Mexico, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and parts of Northern Africa. [5] The report warns that 21 of the world's 37 major aquifers are being depleted faster than they can be replenished. [7] Specifically, in the U.S., the High Plains aquifer, which supports over $35 billion in crops, is under threat, with projections indicating that 40% of its area may not support irrigation by 2100 if current extraction rates continue. [7] The report emphasizes the interconnected nature of these risks, where the depletion of groundwater not only threatens food security but also has cascading effects on ecosystems and social stability.

The Trump administration's order aims to allow for the 2.5 gallons per minute standard to be applied to each individual nozzle on a showerhead. A White House fact sheet stated the move was to "end the Obama-Biden war on water pressure and make America's showers great again." This action is part of a broader effort by the administration to roll back environmental regulations and what it terms "overregulation." More specifically, the report found that about 27 million of these individuals live in areas experiencing a 'high degree of local water stress.' The assessment, which analyzed data from 2010 to 2020, integrated water quantity, quality, and usage patterns to create a more complete picture of water availability. A key finding highlighted that socially vulnerable populations have a disproportionately higher risk of facing water limitations. metadata.original_text: This time series records water scarcity data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-12-21 to 2026-03-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The National Integrated Drought Information System (NIDIS) reported that as of December 7, snow cover across the Western United States fell to 90,646 square miles. This marks the lowest December 7 snow cover amount in the MODIS satellite record since at least 2001, significantly exacerbating the regional snow drought. <2> On November 19, 2025, the Arizona Water Infrastructure Finance Authority (WIFA) board voted unanimously to approve taxpayer funding to explore four long-term water augmentation proposals. Intended to combat the state's severe water challenges stemming from stressed groundwater supplies and Colorado River cutbacks, the approved proposals include plans by private companies to develop desalination plants in California and Mexico. The funding advances these projects into a study phase where WIFA will evaluate engineering options, regulatory requirements, financial approaches, and environmental impacts to determine if they can deliver reliable new water supplies for Arizona. <3> On November 12, 2025, the Nevada Irrigation District (NID) Board of Directors officially lifted its emergency water shortage declaration. The decision was made after Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) completed critical infrastructure repairs, including returning the Spaulding 1 powerhouse to service on July 24, 2025, which successfully restored water flows through the Drum Canal system and allowed reservoir levels to rebound. <4> Rain Enhancement Technologies Holdco, Inc. (NASDAQ:RAIN) announced on November 11, 2025, that it has commenced operations of its first U.S. weather enhancement system in Gill, Colorado. The system, called the Weather Enhancement Technology Array (WETA), was installed in October 2025 and is now fully operational under a permit from the State of Colorado's Water Conservation Board. This project marks Colorado's first warm-weather modification program. The technology is designed to increase rainfall for agricultural land by utilizing a solar-powered, chemical-free atmospheric ionization process. The WETA system is intended to cover approximately 360 square miles of farmland in Weld County, with peer-reviewed trials indicating a potential to boost precipitation by 15% to 18%. <5> On October 19, 2025, Texas Governor Greg Abbott amended and renewed a disaster proclamation for 57 counties due to persistent and exceptional drought conditions. This action was a continuation of an initial proclamation from July 8, 2022, and was based on confirmation from the Texas Division of Emergency Management that severe drought conditions continued to pose a threat of imminent disaster. The proclamation authorizes the use of all available state and political subdivision resources to address the disaster and allows for the suspension of any regulatory statutes or rules that might impede emergency response efforts. <6> 'Imagine a Day Without Water' is a national day of action held to raise public awareness about the essential role water plays in daily life and to highlight the critical need for investment in the nation's aging water infrastructure. Organized by the US Water Alliance's Value of Water Campaign, the event brings together diverse participants, including communities, policymakers, businesses, and educators, to emphasize that water is an invaluable resource. The day of action encourages people to consider the widespread consequences of a lack of water, which would impact everything from personal hygiene and public health to the functioning of businesses, hospitals, and emergency services like firefighting. A key goal of the campaign is to advocate for sustainable and robust investment to ensure that all communities have equitable access to safe and affordable water for future generations. <7> On October 6, 2025, the Pennsylvania Drought Task Force officially declared a 'Drought Watch' for 25 counties following a period of low rainfall over the summer. The specific counties impacted are Beaver, Bradford, Butler, Cambria, Cameron, Clarion, Clearfield, Clinton, Crawford, Elk, Erie, Forest, Indiana, Jefferson, Lawrence, Lycoming, McKean, Mercer, Potter, Schuylkill, Somerset, Tioga, Venango, Warren, and Washington. In the announcement, DEP Secretary Jessica Shirley noted the dry conditions and urged residents of the affected areas to voluntarily decrease their water usage by 5 to 10 percent. <8> The U.S. government entered a shutdown on October 1, 2025, after Congress failed to pass an appropriations bill for the new fiscal year. In response, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) activated its updated contingency plan, which called for a significant reduction in operations. Out of its 15,166 employees, only 1,734 were slated to continue working to handle legally required duties. Consequently, many critical activities for the water sector, such as issuing new grants and permits, conducting civil enforcement inspections, and approving state requests, were halted. However, essential services, including emergency and disaster assistance, law enforcement, criminal investigations, and urgent Superfund response work, were set to continue. <9> A federal judge ruled that a lawsuit filed by residents of Flint, Michigan, against the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) for its role in the city's water crisis could proceed, denying the agency's petition to dismiss the case.
